hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Statins delay death by only a few days, on average, in the trials that tested them.

These drugs are widely prescribed to lower LDL cholesterol and to reduce the chance of a heart attack or stroke. Yet for most people taking them, the absolute benefit is small, and the outcome that matters most, living longer, is where the trial data are thinnest.

A review of 11 large statin trials measured the average delay in death over two to six years of treatment. In people who had not yet had a heart attack or stroke, death was delayed by only a few days. In people who already had heart disease, the median was 4.1 days, and some trials showed slightly shorter survival on the drug. And that is an average, so many people gained nothing at all.

Muscle symptoms are commonly reported by people taking these drugs. In an observational study of people on high-dose statin therapy, about 1 in 10 reported muscle symptoms, and some surveys put that share closer to 1 in 4.

In a large observational study of more than 150,000 postmenopausal women, statin use was linked to a 48% higher risk of developing diabetes. In a two-month controlled trial, atorvastatin raised fasting insulin by 25% to 45%.

A person weighing a few extra days of life against muscle pain and a higher diabetes risk deserves to see those numbers side by side.
hits.draft_en:
Ben Bikman put the statin numbers side by side, and they're worth a look.

He cites a review of 11 big trials: in people who hadn't had a heart attack or stroke, statins delayed death by only a few days on average. In people with heart disease, the median was 4.1 days. He also lists muscle aches reported by roughly 1 in 10 on high doses, and a higher diabetes risk in some studies.

I'm not telling anyone to stop their tablets. Don't do that off a post. But you're allowed to ask your doctor for the real numbers for someone like you, and weigh them up yourself.

I'm increasingly convinced that maintaining high aerobic fitness may be one of the most important things we can do for brain aging.

Brain MRI research has linked higher aerobic fitness with less grey-matter shrinkage across the lifespan in a region involved in attention and working memory. Older age was associated with smaller gray matter volume there among less fit adults, but not more fit adults. Larger volume in that region was also linked to better cognitive scores.

Long-term observational evidence has associated each 1-MET improvement in estimated fitness with a 16% lower risk of dementia. Separate exercise studies have reported increased glucose uptake in brain regions vulnerable to early Alzheimer’s-related changes after HIIT, and improved brain blood flow after aerobic training.

VO2 max is a capacity we can measure and train, which is why I keep coming back to intervals like the Norwegian 4x4. Taken together, these findings make aerobic capacity hard to ignore.

Recommendations about saturated fat have been dramatically oversimplified.

Dr. Dariush Mozaffarian argues that saturated fat can become a distraction when it’s the only thing we use to judge a food.

Foods with similar saturated fat content can affect the body differently. For example, saturated fat from butter raises LDL cholesterol, while the same amount from cream can produce little to no increase.

One possible explanation is the milk fat globule membrane, the natural coating around fat droplets in cream, largely absent from butter oil. The structure surrounding the fat influences its biological effects.

Recommendations that reduce a food to a single number of fat grams can miss its structure, its other components (the food matrix), and the overall diet it belongs to. Those details matter when translating nutrition research into advice about what to eat.

From the latest episode of the podcast. You can find it on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Insulin resistance is closely tied to low testosterone in men, and the drop appears to come from the testes themselves.

A lot of men with low testosterone are told it's just age, or they're handed a prescription without anyone asking why the number fell. Low testosterone and insulin resistance show up together so often that it's worth asking which one is pushing the other.

One research group studied men across a range of metabolic health, from normal blood sugar through prediabetes to type 2 diabetes, and measured how well insulin worked in each of them with the most precise method available. The more insulin resistant a man was, the lower his testosterone.

They also studied the hormone pathway step by step. Testosterone production starts in the brain, which sends luteinizing hormone to the testes and tells the Leydig cells there to make testosterone. In these men, the brain's signal looked normal no matter how insulin resistant they were. The difference showed up when the testes were stimulated directly. The more insulin resistant men produced far less testosterone in response to the same stimulation.

This finding points to the testes themselves. The signal arrives, but the cells that make testosterone respond poorly when insulin isn't working well.

I've studied ceramides for years, and I'm convinced they're the primary molecular driver of insulin resistance. So I was glad to read this new Perspective from Eric Hajduch and Hervé Le Stunff, looking back on 25 years of ceramide research.

The story starts with a puzzle. People with obesity and type 2 diabetes store more fat inside their muscle cells, yet endurance athletes store just as much and stay highly insulin sensitive. That pushed the field past fat storage itself and toward specific fat-derived molecules, and ceramides rose to the top.

Ceramides are made from saturated fats like palmitate. Inside the cell, they block insulin's signal by shutting down Akt, a key protein insulin relies on to move glucose into muscle.

The review also lays out where the field is heading. Where ceramides sit inside the cell matters as much as how much of them there is. Ceramides at the cell membrane, where insulin's signal begins, appear to do the most harm. Certain types, especially C16 and C18 ceramides, are the ones most often tied to impaired insulin action in muscle.

That has real implications for treatment. Future therapies could keep harmful ceramides away from insulin's signaling machinery while leaving the cell's useful sphingolipids alone.

Thanks to the authors for a thoughtful look at a field I care deeply about.

Postmenopausal women with the highest fasting insulin have a clearly higher risk of breast cancer, and that holds true even after their estrogen levels are taken into account.

For years, the main explanation for why obesity raises breast cancer risk after menopause has been estrogen, since fat tissue keeps making estrogen after the ovaries slow down, and that explanation has real merit because estrogen drives the growth of many breast tumors. What it leaves out is insulin, which is a powerful growth signal in its own right and tends to run high in people carrying excess body fat.

This fits what's known about breast tissue and tumors. Insulin tells cells to grow and divide, and many breast tumors carry far more insulin receptors than normal breast tissue, which leaves them well equipped to respond when insulin stays high day after day.

It also means a woman with a normal body weight but chronically high insulin isn't necessarily protected, while a woman who brings her insulin down may be lowering a risk that her scale would never show.

Weight loss in older adults can cost them muscle and bone they can't afford to lose, and the type of exercise paired with the diet has a large influence on how much of that tissue they end up losing.

Losing fat helps an older person with obesity move more easily and lowers their metabolic risk, but dieting also takes muscle and bone at a stage of life when both are already declining with age, so an older person who loses too much muscle while dieting can end up lighter on the scale yet weaker and more fragile than before.

In a clinical trial, older adults with obesity were all placed on the same weight loss program and assigned to aerobic exercise, resistance training, or a combination of both, while a control group made no changes, and all three exercise groups lost about the same amount of weight.

What they lost, however, was quite different. Those doing only aerobic exercise lost the most lean mass and the most bone at the hip, while adding resistance training substantially reduced those losses, and the group doing both types of exercise improved their physical function the most, gaining strength from the lifting and fitness from the aerobic work.

This makes sense because muscle responds to load. When calories are cut, the body breaks down tissue to make up the difference, and muscle that isn't being worked hard is broken down more readily than muscle that is regularly asked to lift something heavy, which gives the body a reason to hold on to it. Bone responds to mechanical stress in much the same way, which is why the hip held up better in the groups that lifted.

If an older person wants to lose fat without becoming frailer, combining resistance training with aerobic exercise, along with eating enough protein, gives them the best chance of keeping their muscle and bone while actually getting stronger.

In the middle of a famine, Hansel and Gretel got left in the woods so the rest of the family might have enough to eat. They wandered for days with almost nothing. Then they found a little house made of bread, with a cake roof and windows of clear sugar. They didn’t stop to think. Hansel started pulling pieces off the roof. Gretel bit into the sugar panes. It was the sweetest thing either of them had ever tasted.

That house was the trap. The witch built it so hungry kids would stop and eat, and then she could take them.

In the medieval world this story comes from, actual sugar was rare and expensive. It came from the East and only the rich ever got much of it—kings and nobles buying it by the sack for fancy feasts and medicines. Ordinary people mostly used honey. Still, the people who could get sugar wanted more of it. It was sweet in a way honey wasn’t, and once you had it you kept looking for it. Demand kept growing.

So for two starving kids, a whole house with sugar windows wasn’t just food. It was something almost impossible to walk past. The sweetness hit harder because they’d never had anything like it. They walked right in. They got out later by outsmarting the witch, but the bait worked exactly the way it was meant to. Even back then, when sugar was scarce and costly, it already had a way of making people ignore the danger for one more bite.

We’ve made that bait cheap and everywhere. Modern sugar intake has driven up obesity, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and tooth decay on a scale no medieval person could have imagined. The same sweetness that once lured two kids into a witch’s house now quietly damages the health of whole populations, one easy bite at a time.

A lot of people think there's a real health benefit to drinking extra liters of water every day that they don't want and their body doesn't need.

We've all been told to drink at least eight 8-ounce glasses a day, and some people push a gallon or sip on a big jug all day whether they're thirsty or not.

For a healthy person living an ordinary life, this is not healthier and is potentially harmful.

In 2002, Dr. Heinz Valtin at Dartmouth Medical School published a review of the eight glasses rule and couldn't find a single study that supported it.

One suggested origin is a 1945 government statement that adults need about 2.5 liters of water a day. The very next sentence said most of that water is already in the food we eat, and that part seems to have been forgotten.

In 2004 the Institute of Medicine said the vast majority of healthy people meet their daily water needs by letting thirst be their guide, and they chose not to give any number of glasses to drink.

The amounts they listed, about 91 ounces a day for women and 125 ounces for men, are what hydrated people were already taking in. That counts every drink, including coffee and tea, plus the water in food, which supplies about a fifth of it.

In a 6-month randomized trial, 141 healthy men aged 55 to 75 were told to drink about 6 extra glasses of water a day. Most of them couldn't manage that much, and their blood pressure, blood sodium, kidney function, and quality of life didn't change.

In 631 adults whose kidneys were already weakened, coaching them to drink more water for a year didn't slow the loss of kidney function compared with people who kept drinking their usual amount, so extra water isn't flushing your kidneys into better health.

A 2024 review found only 18 randomized trials of drinking more water, and the authors wrote that the benefits of increasing water intake are not well established.

The benefits showed up only in narrow groups, like people who have already had a kidney stone, women with repeated bladder infections who were drinking very little to begin with, and a few small trials of overweight adults who drank about two glasses of water right before meals.

Forcing water past your thirst can also hurt you. At the 2002 Boston Marathon, 13 percent of the 488 runners who had blood drawn at the finish line had low blood sodium, and the runners who gained weight during the race, which means they drank more than they sweated out, had about four times the odds of it.

So drink when you're thirsty and stop when you're not. On hot days or when you're working hard and sweating, you'll get thirstier and drink more.

outsiders.name: @levelsio
outsiders.text:
There wasn't much technology to work with in terms of interior design with my app 🏡 Interior AI the last 12 months

For 4 years it's been based on simple image models: photos of your interior as input -> redesigns out as output

But now there is a completely new dimension to it 😬

As you probably saw on your timeline, AI can finally generate headless Blender 3d scenes from just a rough video (which I did today of my living room), or even a few photos, and even a floorplan (which no image model was able to understand before, believe me I tried 100 times!)

That means that 3d scene I can then make fully editable in my app Interior AI

Meaning you can paint any wall, floor or ceiling any color, next move around, delete or add new furniture etc from a giant 3d library of furniture

Endless possibilities!!

I think I found my next big feature 😍

I'll try get something live in Interior AI within the next few hours!!!

outsiders.name: @levelsio
outsiders.text:
Okay it works, I can now upload a video or some photos or just a floor plan of my living room

And then:
- empty it fully
- move around furniture
- remove furniture
- paint the walls, floor, ceiling and any object in any color

Next:
- top down floor plan view
- change to any interior design style with one-click
- integrate it into 🏡 Interior AI fully as a feature

Very very very cool 😍🤟

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: You can’t fight the second law of thermodynamics. The perplexity of the universe is destined to increase.

outsiders.name: @levelsio
outsiders.text:
⏰ 3 hours later I have it working as a feature!

Real video-to-3d with my own built headless Blender on a VPS

You can upload a walkthrough video of your living room or entire floor

Interior AI turns it into a walkable 3d space where you can paint your walls, move everything around and get a floor plan

It's a quick prototype but it works!

LIVE now on 🏡 Interior AI for all users 😊 🙏 

Thanks @wesbos for a lot of the inspiration here too
